name: Tail
blurb: The bottom of the ship: the thrust structure, the engines, steering, strap-on boosters, fins and landing legs.

rows.name: Thrust structure
rows.role: The frame the engines push on. It sets how many engines there are and how they are arranged.

rows.name: Engines
rows.role: One type for the whole cluster. Required.

rows.name: Steering
rows.role: How the engine thrust is pointed: swivelling the engine, small vernier chambers, or vanes in the jet.

rows.name: Strap-on boosters
rows.role: Solid or liquid boosters clamped to the side: extra thrust off the pad.

rows.name: Fins & fairings
rows.role: Keep the ship pointing nose-first in thick air; fairings smooth the air over outer engines.

rows.name: Landing gear
rows.role: Legs or airbags for the touchdown on Mars.

shapes.name: One big engine
shapes.real: Redstone, Delta II core (one main engine, four fins)
shapes.desc: One large engine on a conical thrust frame, four fins and four graphite jet vanes in the exhaust to steer, as on the Redstone: the classic layout of the first rockets, and still the cheapest way to lift a ship. Real tails carry no landing legs: add them in the Landing gear row.
cons: No engine-out: one failure ends the flight

shapes.name: One engine + three solids
shapes.desc: One large engine helped off the pad by three solid motors around the base. Delta II flew 155 times with three, four or nine of them; this is the three-solid version.
cons: Falls about 170 m/s short of Mars with the Reliable body: add a tank
Solid casings stay on as dead mass
No engine-out

shapes.name: Boattail + two big solids
shapes.desc: One big kerosene engine whose top hides in a tapering boattail skirt, with two large graphite solids. Atlas V flies with none to five solids; this is the two-solid version; Boeing's Starliner flies the two-solid N22.
pros: Engine plumbing shielded from the airflow
cons: Falls about 130 m/s short of Mars with the Reliable body: add a tank
Solid casings stay on as dead mass
No engine-out

shapes.name: Wide core + two big solids
shapes.desc: A wide core with one hydrogen engine between two huge segmented solid boosters, which do most of the lifting for the first two minutes. Ariane 5 flew 117 times, including the James Webb Space Telescope.
cons: Falls about 140 m/s short of Mars with the Reliable body: add a tank
Two 3.2 t booster casings stay on as dead mass
No engine-out

shapes.name: Two engines side by side
shapes.real: Titan II GLV (LR87: two chambers), the Gemini launcher
shapes.desc: Two large engines on one cross-beam: twice the thrust of the single-engine tail without boosters. Titan II launched all ten crewed Gemini missions.
pros: Twice the thrust, no boosters to carry
cons: Falls about 510 m/s short of Mars with the Reliable body: add a tank; two heavy engines eat Δv
No engine-out: either failure ends the flight

shapes.name: Two engines + two solids
shapes.desc: Two methane engines side by side with a pair of big solids. Vulcan can fly with none, two, four or six; this is the two-solid version.
pros: Medium engines keep the price down
cons: Falls about 220 m/s short of Mars with the Reliable body: add a tank
Solid casings stay on as dead mass
No engine-out

shapes.name: Three engines + two big solids
shapes.real: Space Shuttle (three RS-25, two four-segment SRBs)
shapes.desc: Three hydrogen engines in a triangle between two huge segmented solid boosters, scaled down to fit. The boosters do most of the lifting; the three engines can lose one and still fly.
cons: Falls about 240 m/s short of Mars with the Reliable body: add a tank
Two 3.2 t booster casings stay on as dead mass
Three engines to buy

shapes.name: Four chambers + four liquid boosters
shapes.real: Soyuz (R-7 family: core RD-108A, four RD-107A boosters)
shapes.desc: A core with four chambers and steering verniers, ringed by four cone-topped liquid boosters: the R-7 cross that launched Gagarin and every Soyuz since.
pros: Liquid boosters: far better Isp than solids, reaches Mars with the Reliable body
Proven: the R-7 family has flown more than 1,900 times
cons: Reliability only about 81 %: four boosters and four chambers must all work
Four booster shells stay on as dead mass
Only just fits the budget with the Reliable body

shapes.name: Five engines, fairings and fins
shapes.real: Saturn V first stage S-IC (five F-1)
shapes.desc: Four steering engines at the corners of a square around a fixed fifth, each outer engine under a fairing with a big fin. The tail of the Moon rocket, scaled down.
pros: Very stable: four big fins low down
cons: Five medium engines cost about $3.0M: about $0.5M over budget with the Reliable body
Small pumps are affordable but cannot lift a full ship (TWR 0.7)
Falls about 850 m/s short of Mars with the Reliable body: add a tank

shapes.name: Seven engines
shapes.desc: Six methane engines in a ring around a seventh under a wide base, on folding legs. Seven medium engines push like two large ones and survive the loss of one.
cons: Seven medium engines cost about $4.3M: about $1.6M over budget with the Reliable body
Small pumps cannot lift a full ship (TWR 0.9)
Falls about 1,080 m/s short of Mars with the Reliable body: add a tank

shapes.name: Nine engines (Octaweb)
shapes.desc: Nine engines, eight in a ring around one, under a base heat shield, with carbon legs folded along the tail. Nine small engines push like one large one; on a light ship (as on Rocket Lab's Electron) they lift briskly.
pros: Nine small engines cost about $2.4M: the Reliable ship stays under budget
Can lose one engine and fly on
cons: Nine small engines (850 kN at sea level) only just lift the Reliable ship: TWR 1.18, under the 1.2 needed. Medium pumps lift it at TWR 3.2, but the ship then costs about $7.7M
Falls about 410 m/s short of Mars with the Reliable body: add a tank
